# Goal & Rider Author

A two-document pattern for briefing an autonomous coding agent
(Claude Code, Codex CLI, or any agentic harness) on the next round of
work. The **goal**
is the ≤4000-char spine: what to do, what to read first, the posture,
the verification, the stop conditions. The **rider** holds the
prescriptive detail: data schemas, phase plans, depth-test names,
verb signatures, error footers, out-of-scope lists.

The pattern's superpower is that the goal stays small enough to paste
into a Codex `/goal` or a Claude run prompt, while the rider can be
arbitrarily detailed without bloating the executor's working memory.

This skill is project-agnostic. It works for any codebase that has a
`docs/goals/` (or equivalent) directory, conventional commits, and
some form of AS-BUILT / architecture doc. Substitute the project's
own toolchain commands wherever the templates say
`<project's ... command>`.

## When to invoke

The user is about to start a new round of agentic work and wants
goal+rider files written into a project's `docs/goals/` directory.
Triggers include "draft a goal that addresses X", "write a goal+rider
for Y", "new goal for the next agentic turn", "rider for X".

## Pre-work — do not skip

Before drafting, gather context. Read in this order, skipping items
the project doesn't have:

1. **Project architecture doc** — `AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md`,
   `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, or whatever the project
   uses. Look for a "what's shipped vs thin" section if one exists;
   it grounds the goal in reality.
2. **Prior goal+rider pairs** in `docs/goals/` (or wherever the
   project keeps them). Their invariants compose forward; do not
   duplicate verbatim. Skim the most recent two pairs to absorb
   voice and section conventions.
3. **Recent commits**: `git log --oneline -30 -- docs/goals/` and
   `git log --oneline -30`. Reveals delivery cadence and the
   conventional-commit format the project uses.
4. **Source code at HEAD** for any data structures, file paths, or
   function names you'll quote in the rider. Verify they match HEAD
   before citing.
5. **Research or pain-point reports** the project has (e.g.,
   unmet-needs, user-research, retro docs). They ground the
   ergonomics in real pain.

If you can't find prior pairs or an architecture doc, **ask the user**
for a pointer — don't invent one.

## Goal document recipe (≤4000 chars)

**Path:** `<project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-goal.md`

The `<HHMM>` is the local 24-hour clock time when the file is created
(e.g., `1444` for 2:44 PM). It makes `ls docs/goals/` sort in true
authoring order rather than alphabetical by topic. When two pairs land
within the same minute, secondary alphabetical sort handles the tiebreak;
that's fine.

**Hard cap:** `wc -c <file>` must be ≤4000 (prior precedents: 3929–4112).
Re-check after every edit pass. Note the `-HHMM-` insert costs ~5 chars
per internal rider reference, so leave a small buffer when riders cross-cite.

**Skeleton** — fill each section, cut to fit:

```markdown
GOAL: <one-sentence headline>. <one paragraph: current pain → what the goal lands → headline word (Friendliness / Multi-agent / Self-documenting / Default mode / …)>.

**Read first.**

- `<absolute path to project architecture doc>` — substrate; one line.
- `<absolute path to the rider being written>` — schemas, signatures, depth tests.
- `<absolute paths to exemplars or research reports>` — grounding.
- Prior riders in `<absolute path to docs/goals/>` — invariants hold.

**Posture.** Stays `<tier>`. No `<struct>` schema changes (if applicable). No `git push`. Edits inside `<project root>`. Major architectural decisions → `<V1-CANDIDATES path>`.

<DOMAIN BODY — one or two of these, depending on the goal:>

**<N> modes / verbs / artifacts, auto-resolved.**

- **`<name>`** — <one line of behavior>.

**New verbs.**

- `<verb> <args>` — <one line>.

**Friendliness as a verifiable contract.**

- Auto-detect, don't ask (the obvious case is the default).
- Preflight + preview before any state change.
- Refuse with `try: <command>` lines.
- Rollback is one command.
- Lifecycle hints after every action.

**Phases.** Eleven (P1–P11) in the rider. Each: depth test first → implement → `<project's build+test+lint+fmt command>` green → conventional-commit → CHANGELOG. P11 adds a `<new section>` to the project architecture doc.

**Verification.**

- Commands green every commit; every rider depth test present and passing.
- <Smoke 1>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- <Smoke 2>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- No edits outside `<project>`. No `git push`. No schema changes.

**Stop when** verification passes, AS-BUILT updated, CHANGELOG has a "<Milestone name> (alpha)" section, committed locally.

```

GOAL: Let one task spawn N orchestrators. Add `deadreckon campaign <goal> --n <2..=6>`: a **meta-coordinator** that decomposes a root goal into N independent sub-goals, launches each as its own full orchestrator (`orchestrate full-plan`) in an isolated scope, then composes the N merged results into one promoted run. It is the existing `fork`->`merge` pattern lifted exactly one level: each child is a sub-orchestrator whose merged result is itself a normal run, so the meta-merge reuses the same compose primitives. Bounded by a **hard depth cap of 2**, a **tree-wide spend ceiling**, a **cycle guard**, and a **gate-verdict roll-up** so nesting cannot quietly erode the §35 tamper-evident gate. Headline word: **Campaign**.

**Read first.**

- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md` — §30 plans/orchestration, §35 tamper-evident gate.
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/2026-05-28-1841-deadreckon-campaign-rider.md` — full contract.
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/plan.rs`, `.../src/tamper.rs`.
- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs` — `fork_command`, `run_plan_child`, `merge_command`, `compose_plan_merge_working`, `resolve_plan_result_run`, `kill_command`.
- Prior riders in `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/` — invariants hold.

**Posture.** Production-release track. Files-not-fields: meta-plan, lineage, and roll-up are new files under `~/.deadreckon/plans/<campaign-id>/`; **no** `Plan`/`PlanTask`/`PipelineState`/provider schema changes. Child work stays normal `deadreckon` subprocesses (§30.1). Depth **hard-capped at 2** — sub-orchestrators cannot fan out again. No `git push`. Edits inside `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`. Depth>2, cross-level dependencies/merge-repair, recursive live attach → `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`.

**User contract.**

- `deadreckon campaign <goal> --n <2..=6>` previews mode, N, depth cap, tree budget, and provider roles, then (with `--yes`) launches N independent sub-orchestrators and composes their results.
- A campaign invoked from inside a sub-orchestrator (depth would reach 2) is **refused**; no meta-plan is written. A sub-goal resolving to an ancestor's `task_key`/scope is **refused** (cycle guard).
- `--max-spend` is a **tree ceiling**: split across sub-orchestrators, aggregate spend tracked across every leaf run; the meta refuses to launch more once exhausted.
- The campaign result reports **clean only if every leaf run signed clean**; any refused leaf fails the campaign, any caveat leaf surfaces a caveat (roll-up over §35 verdicts).
- `attach <campaign-id>` shows the N sub-plan rows with a breadcrumb; `kill <campaign-id>` cascades to sub-coordinators and their children; `show <campaign-id> --why-failed` explains a failed campaign.

**Phases.** Eleven (P1-P11) in the rider. Each: depth test first -> implement -> focused tests green -> conventional local commit -> CHANGELOG. P1 lands the depth/cycle/lineage guard (RED first). P11 adds AS-BUILT §36 and logs deferrals.

**Verification.**

- Every rider depth test present and passing; `cargo fmt --check`; `git diff --check`.
- Smoke (smoke provider, `--sandbox none`): a 2-sub-goal campaign launches two sub-orchestrators, composes one promoted result, and `campaign-rollup.json` records both leaf verdicts.
- Smoke: a campaign attempted at depth 2 is **refused** (no meta-plan, clear reason).
- Smoke: one leaf refused (hollow pass) makes the **campaign fail**, never `Completed`; one leaf caveat surfaces a caveat on the meta summary.
- No edits outside the repo; no `git push`; no `Plan`/`PlanTask`/`PipelineState` schema changes.

**Stop when** verification passes, campaign launches N orchestrators within the depth cap and tree budget, the meta-merge produces one promoted run, the gate roll-up refuses on any leaf refusal, attach/kill/why-failed work for campaigns, AS-BUILT and CHANGELOG record the behavior, deferrals are in V1-CANDIDATES, and the work is committed locally.

# deadreckon — Orchestrate Campaign Rider (one task spawns N orchestrators, depth-capped at 2)

This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at
`/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/2026-05-28-1841-deadreckon-campaign-goal.md`.
It supersedes nothing in prior riders (notably
`2026-05-11-1444-deadreckon-orchestrate-rider.md`,
`2026-05-16-1122-deadreckon-semantic-merge-repair-rider.md`,
`2026-05-18-2226-deadreckon-orchestration-eventbus-rider.md`,
`2026-05-28-1556-deadreckon-tamper-evident-gate-rider.md`) — their invariants
still apply. This rider adds a **campaign** layer: a meta-coordinator that spawns N
independent full orchestrators one level down, composes their merged results into a
single promoted run, and rolls their §35 gate verdicts up to the top.

**All paths absolute.** Source `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`, runtime `~/.deadreckon/`.

## The idea in one paragraph (read before designing)

deadreckon already has the whole machine. `fork_command` (`main.rs:13217`) launches
N child *runs* as `deadreckon run` subprocesses, each isolated by
`DEADRECKON_SCOPE_ROOT` to a per-task launch dir (`run_plan_child`,
`main.rs:15934–15984`). `merge_command` (`main.rs:16362`) composes those children's
**library artifacts** into one promoted run (`compose_plan_merge_working`,
`main.rs:16698`), and that merged run is a *normal run* resolvable by id
(`resolve_plan_result_run`, `main.rs:13733`; AS-BUILT §30.4). **Campaign is the same
pattern lifted one level:** the meta-coordinator launches N `orchestrate full-plan`
subprocesses instead of N `run` subprocesses; each sub-orchestrator does its own
plan→fork→merge and produces a normal merged result run; the meta-merge composes
those N result runs with the *same* compose primitive. Nothing in the spawn,
isolation, or merge substrate needs reinventing — the work is the **meta layer and
its guardrails**.

## Posture (decided — do not redesign)

- **Production-release track.** Release-grade orchestration, not a toy.
- **Files-not-fields.** New durable state is files under
  `~/.deadreckon/plans/<campaign-id>/`: `campaign.json`, `campaign-coordinator.json`,
  `lineage.json`, `campaign-rollup.json`, `campaign-events.jsonl`,
  sub-plan launch sidecars. **No** new fields on `Plan`, `PlanTask`,
  `PipelineState`, `AcceptanceMarker`, or provider config. Sub-orchestrators
  produce ordinary `Plan`s and ordinary merged runs that existing code already
  handles.
- **Depth hard-capped at 2.** A campaign is depth 0; the orchestrators it spawns are
  depth 1; those orchestrators **must refuse** to fan out again (would be depth 2).
  The cap is a constant `CAMPAIGN_MAX_DEPTH: u32 = 2` — not configurable in this goal.
- **Independent sub-goals only.** Sub-goals carry **no cross-sub dependencies** in
  this goal (each sub-orchestrator is a parallel island). Cross-level dependency
  edges are a V1 candidate.
- **Reuse, don't fork.** Factor shared logic out of `compose_plan_merge_working` and
  `run_plan_child` rather than copying them. New code is the meta layer only.
- **Trust composes downward.** Every leaf run still goes through its own §35
  tamper-evident gate unchanged. The campaign adds *aggregation*, never a bypass.
- **No `git push`.** Phased local commits only.
- **No V1 invention.** Depth>2, cross-level merge-repair, recursive live attach,
  provider-planned dependency graphs across levels → `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
- **Edits stay inside `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`.**

## Vocabulary (use exactly)

- **campaign** — the meta operation / its plan file (`campaign.json`). The
  user-facing verb is the **top-level** `deadreckon campaign`, a peer to

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about Rust Clippy pedantic and nursery lints worth enabling in 2025:

## Pedantic Lints

The `clippy::pedantic` group makes Clippy even more pedantic and is for Clippy power users that want an in depth check of their code. However, instead of enabling the whole group, you may want to cherry-pick lints out of the pedantic group, and if you enable this group, expect to also use `#[allow]` attributes generously throughout your code.

The lints worth enabling include checks for unintentional integer casts, missing panic documentation, and needlessly complex boolean expressions.

Common pedantic lints that projects selectively enable include:
- `cast_precision_loss`
- `missing_errors_doc`
- `missing_panics_doc`
- `module_name_repetitions`
- `must_use_candidate`
- `struct_excessive_bools`

## Nursery Lints

The `clippy::nursery` group contains lints which are buggy or need more work, and it is not recommended to enable the whole group, but rather cherry-pick lints that are useful for your code base and your use case. The nursery group contains experimental lints that may still change but are already useful on stable code.

## Configuration Approach

Library crates SHOULD enable pedantic lints, and you should configure lint levels in Cargo.toml, not with scattered allow attributes. A recommended configuration pattern includes selectively enabling these groups while allowing specific lints that are too strict for your project.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about Rust idioms for reducing clones, allocations, and best practices with iterators versus index loops:

## Key Findings

### Iterators vs Index Loops

Rust's iterator chains optimize better than manual loops: iterators eliminate bounds checks and enable LLVM to apply vectorization and other optimizations that manual loops prevent. Rust's iterators are zero-cost abstractions, often outperforming manual loops due to compiler optimizations.

### Reducing Clones

Cloning is convenient but expensive; use references and borrowing instead of cloning the entire data structure. .iter() creates an iterator that borrows each element of the vector, which is more efficient than using `.into_iter()` when you want to preserve the collection.

### Avoiding Unnecessary Allocations

Iterator::collect converts an iterator into a collection such as Vec, which typically requires an allocation, and you should avoid calling collect if the collection is then only iterated over again. Avoid unnecessary allocations by using methods like .for_each() for side effects or .sum()/.fold() for aggregation.

### Iterator Optimization Techniques

cloned() produces a clone of all of the items in the original iterator; this is particularly useful with iterators over &Item references. For better performance, copied() produces a copy of all of the items in the original iterator and is likely to be faster than cloned() if the Item type implements Copy.

### Best Practices

It is often better to return an iterator type like impl Iterator<Item=T> from a function than a Vec<T>, which avoids unnecessary allocations at function boundaries.

Based on the search results, here's what you need to know about Rust module organization for 2024:

## Current Best Practice: File as Module (Non-mod.rs)

Prior to rustc 1.30, using mod.rs files was the way to load a module with nested children, but it is encouraged to use the new naming convention as it is more consistent, and avoids having many files named mod.rs within a project.

The Rust community has turned away from the mod.rs file, and now encourages the use of ./module + ./module.rs approach instead.

## How It Works

When you declare a module, the compiler looks for my_module.rs or my_module/mod.rs in the same directory. So you can structure your code two ways:

1. **Modern approach (preferred)**: `module.rs` alongside a `module/` directory for submodules
2. **Legacy approach**: `module/mod.rs` inside the directory

## For Large Codebases

More complicated projects can have many modules, and they'll need to be organized logically in order to keep track of them. What "logically" means in your project is up to you and depends on how you and your library's users think about your project's domain. Use the techniques shown here to create side-by-side modules and nested modules in whatever structure you would like.

The newer convention reduces clutter by avoiding multiple `mod.rs` files scattered throughout your directory tree, making large projects easier to navigate.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about splitting large files into modules in Rust while maintaining your public API using the re-export facade pattern:

## Key Approach: Module Declaration + Re-exports

To split a large file, remove the code inside the module's curly brackets, leaving only the `mod` declaration, so that your root file (lib.rs or main.rs) contains the module declaration.

The examples or external code don't require changes because the public API of the crate hasn't changed from their perspective.

## The Facade Pattern

This setup is known generally as the facade pattern, and it's pretty ubiquitous in Rust code. Instead of exposing each module, you can use a facade pattern where internal modules are organized separately, while a curated set of items are re-exported at the top level using `pub use`.

## Re-exporting for API Stability

Re-exporting is achieved using the `pub use` statement. The basic pattern looks like:

```rust
mod module_name;  // Declare the module
pub use module_name::item_name;  // Re-export specific items
```

Re-exporting allows you to export types and functions from other modules, simplifying public API design by presenting a curated set of items that users of your library need to see, instead of directly exposing the inner structure of modules.

## File Structure

When you have a directory representing a module, the file `src/module_name/mod.rs` contains the code for the module itself, including declarations of its submodules.

This approach allows you to maintain backward compatibility while reorganizing your codebase into separate files.

## Key Patterns for Organizing Large CLIs with Clap Derive

### Use `#[clap(flatten)]` for Code Organization

The `#[clap(flatten)]` attribute flattens inline options from a struct into the parent struct or enum variant, helping break up long series of options into smaller, reusable components that can be more easily processed in different sections of the project's code. For example, Color can be further nested into an OutputOpts struct, defined in a separate output.rs file.

### Structure for Subcommands

Making App an enum with all subcommands has been shown to be problematic because developers often want to introduce global options later. Instead, you can use a struct for your subcommand's arguments with `#[command(subcommand)]` attribute on a field using that type.

### Global Options

Global options are marked with `#[clap(global = true)]`, which means that global options like `--color` can be used anywhere in the command line.

### Subcommand Variants

The Derive API uses `#[derive(Subcommand)]` on enums where each variant represents a distinct subcommand. Each instance of a Subcommand can have its own version, author(s), Args, and even its own subcommands.

### Managing Complexity

For very large CLIs with many nested subcommands, creating a large CLI that involves layers of subcommands can become difficult to manage, and using nested subcommands can get pretty difficult to manage with clap.

Based on the web search results, here's what you should know about the "god main.rs" anti-pattern in Rust CLI projects and how to structure them properly:

## The Anti-Pattern: God main.rs

When starting out with Rust, it's common to place all your code inside a single main.rs file. While this works for small experiments, it quickly becomes messy and hard to maintain as your project grows.

The organizational problem of allocating responsibility for multiple tasks to the main function is common to many binary projects. As a result, many Rust programmers find it useful to split up the separate concerns of a binary program when the main function starts getting large. As a function gains responsibilities, it becomes more difficult to reason about, harder to test, and harder to change without breaking one of its parts.

## Recommended Structure: Separation of Concerns

The recommended pattern is separating concerns: main.rs handles running the program and lib.rs handles all the logic of the task at hand. Because you can't test the main function directly, this structure lets you test all of your program's logic by moving it out of the main function.

## Project Layout for CLI Tools

As your project grows, you'll move most of the logic into separate modules or a lib.rs file, leaving main.rs as a thin entry point.

A typical structure includes:

src/ ├── lib.rs or main.rs # Crate root ├── config.rs # Configuration ├── error.rs # Error types ├── models/ # Data models ├── repositories/ # Data access ├── services/ # Business logic └── utils/ # Helper functions

## Key Principles

- Keep main.rs (or lib.rs) focused on high-level logic and delegate functionality to modules.
- Instead of cramming everything into main.rs, you can group related functions, structs, and enums into separate files or directories.
- With this structure, we have a clean, modular Rust project where business logic, models, and CLI handling are neatly separated.

By splitting business logic into separate modules and keeping main.rs as a thin orchestration layer, you'll have a more maintainable, testable, and scalable CLI application.

## Exit Codes Best Practices

Standardized exit codes should include: SUCCESS (0), GENERAL_ERROR (1), USAGE_ERROR (2), CONFIG_ERROR (3), IO_ERROR (4), PERMISSION_ERROR (5), and NETWORK_ERROR (6). Use meaningful exit codes with zero for success and non-zero for failures.

A common pattern is to have a `determine_exit_code` function that checks for specific error types and returns appropriate exit codes, using error downcasting to identify the error type.

## Argument Validation

Clap provides multiple ways to validate argument values, from compile-time type checking to custom runtime validators. Rust's type system provides the first layer of validation, automatically validating types like `u16`, `PathBuf`, and `IpAddr`.

Clap validates your inputs automatically, catching errors before they become your problem.

## General Best Practices

- Your CLI's `--help` output is your documentation, so use descriptions generously
- If the user makes an error or typo, Clap informs them and exits gracefully, allowing you to make reasonable assumptions about argument validity
- Compile-time guarantees catch errors before users encounter them, so you can focus on application logic rather than argument parsing boilerplate

## Web Search Results for Rust Error Handling 2025

I found comprehensive information about Rust error handling best practices in 2025, particularly regarding the popular error handling libraries and their use cases for libraries versus binaries.

### Key Findings:

**Libraries vs. Binaries Pattern**

Use thiserror to give library consumers clear, matchable error types, and use anyhow to keep application code clean and focused on the happy path. Two crates have emerged as the standard answer: thiserror for libraries and anyhow for applications.

**Why This Distinction Matters**

While anyhow is excellent for application code, it has a limitation: errors are type-erased, which means consumers of your code can't match on specific error types to handle them differently. This is fine for applications (where you typically just log errors), but problematic for libraries where users need to programmatically handle different error cases.

**Eyre as an Alternative**

The eyre crate takes error reporting to another level with customizable formatting, particularly handling error chains with proper indentation and context. It's become a go-to for applications where error messages directly face end users.

**Best Practices**

Always use #[source] or #[from] to preserve the underlying cause, as losing context makes debugging painful. Many projects use both crates: internal libraries use thiserror to define clear error types, while main.rs and top-level application code uses anyhow to aggregate and display them.

**Additional Specialized Tools**

For web services, snafu can be combined with tracing-error, and for CLI tools, miette paired with color-eyre creates exceptional user experiences.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of Rust best practices for avoiding unwrap, expect, and panic, with a focus on result propagation:

## Key Principles

When failure is expected, it's more appropriate to return a Result than to panic, indicating that failure is an expected possibility that the calling code must decide how to handle.

## When NOT to Use unwrap/expect

In production code, especially in library code where the application will likely have a better notion of what to do with the error, you should prefer result propagation, which makes flow control clearer, tends to result in better error messages, and gives the calling functions more options.

unwrap() should not be used for error handling in Rust libraries or applications that are intended for others to use, as using unwrap() for error handling leads to a poor user experience.

## Acceptable Uses for unwrap/expect

There are specific, limited scenarios where these methods are appropriate:

- unwrap and expect are very handy when prototyping and you're not yet ready to decide how to handle errors, as they leave clear markers in your code for when you're ready to make your program more robust.
- In tests, if a method call fails, you'd want the whole test to fail, and calling unwrap or expect is exactly what should happen.
- It's appropriate to call expect when you have some other logic that ensures the Result will have an Ok value, such as parsing a hardcoded valid IP address string.
- Some programmers use unwrap() temporarily while trying to figure out how to solve a problem, then later remove it and add proper error handling before submitting code.

## Recommended Alternatives

### The `?` Operator (Error Propagation)
The ? operator (also known as the try operator) is a powerful tool for propagating errors in a concise and readable way. If the Result is Ok(value), the value is returned; if the Result is Err(error), the error is returned from the enclosing function.

### Using Safer Alternatives
By embracing safer alternatives like match statements, if let, map, and_then, unwrap_or, and the ? operator, you can write more robust, reliable, and maintainable Rust code.

### For expect() Usage
Whenever you use unwrap(), add a comment explaining why you believe it's safe to do so, which helps other developers understand your reasoning and assess the risk.

## Production Code Considerations

It's advisable to avoid using unwrap and expect on external system calls (HTTP calls, RPC, etc.).

The consensus in the Rust community emphasizes that while unwrap and expect have legitimate uses in specific contexts, result propagation via the `?` operator should be your default approach for production code.

I've performed a web search for you on "Rust newtype pattern builder pattern best practices 2025". Here are the key findings:

## Key Concepts

**Newtype Pattern:**
The newtype pattern wraps an existing type in a single-field tuple struct to create a distinct type with zero runtime overhead. The cost at runtime is zero, as the compiler optimises the wrapper away.

**Primary Uses:**
1. **Type Safety:** Use a newtype when mixing two values of the same underlying type would be a bug, such as distances, currencies, ids from different domains, or "validated" vs "raw" inputs.

2. **Reducing Function Argument Bloat:** Without newtypes it's easy to mix up function parameters since multiple parameters might have the same underlying type. With newtypes the compiler catches mistakes — you can't accidentally pass arguments in the wrong order.

3. **Validation:** Newtypes are useful when you want to accept only values that you previously created or when you want to add validation to the value.

**Builder Pattern Integration:**
The typestate pattern is often used with builders — using a builder type, possibly providing methods to set fields, and the final builder::build(self) method would perform validation and return a final validated type. A practical application is a builder that enforces required fields using marker types in the type system to represent state transitions.

**Best Practices:**
If your newtype exists to add type safety or restrict the API, don't implement Deref; if it exists to add capabilities while keeping the inner type's full surface, Deref is the right choice.

Creating new types can result in boilerplate, especially when implementing standard traits or converting back and forth with the base type, so be intentional about trait implementations.

## cargo-machete

cargo-machete is a static analysis tool that identifies unused dependencies in Cargo.toml files by scanning source code for actual usage. It provides a faster, stable-compatible alternative to cargo-udeps, offering a seamless way to reduce project bloat and minimize binary sizes.

### Key Features:
- Works on stable Rust without requiring nightly toolchains
- Includes an automated fix feature to instantly prune unnecessary crates while supporting complex workspace configurations and ignore patterns for false positives like proc-macros
- In the dbsurveyor project, cargo-machete is integrated as a pre-commit hook to automatically detect unused dependencies before code is committed, ensuring continuous dependency hygiene.

### Handling False Positives:
cargo-machete may incorrectly flag dependencies as unused in several scenarios: Derive Macros: Crates like serde_derive or thiserror are used via #[derive()] attributes and never explicitly imported; Proc Macros: Procedural macros used via attributes may not have visible use statements

## cargo-deny

cargo-deny is a linter for Cargo, and there are nice tools that automatically detect dependency issues (hi there cargo-deny).

## Workspace Dependency Management

This approach ensures version consistency across the workspace and makes it easier to identify which dependencies are actually used where. The March 2026 cleanup also introduced cargo-audit configuration to track known security advisories, and removing unused dependencies reduces exposure to security vulnerabilities, even transitive ones.

# Organizing clap Derive Subcommands in Large CLIs

## Core Architecture: App as Struct Above Commands

The guide strongly recommends making `App` a struct that wraps a command enum, rather than making `App` itself an enum. As stated: **"While it is possible to make `App` an enum with all the subcommands, in my experience this design has always come back to bite me."** The reasoning is that this structure anticipates future needs—specifically, the inevitable addition of global options that apply across all subcommands.

## Liberal Use of `#[clap(flatten)]`

Flattening is presented as essential for maintainability. The guide explains that this attribute **"flattens inline options from a struct into the parent struct or enum variant"** and identifies three key benefits:

1. Breaking long option lists into smaller, reusable components
2. Organizing related options in separate files (e.g., an `output.rs` module)
3. Simplifying parameter passing throughout the codebase by bundling complex argument sets

## Global Options Pattern

Options shared across all subcommands should be marked with `#[clap(global = true)]`, allowing them to be specified anywhere on the command line. This separates concerns between global configuration and command-specific arguments.

## Separation Strategy

The recommended structure uses distinct types: `GlobalOpts` struct for shared settings, separate `Args` structs for individual subcommands (like `WriteArgs`), and `ArgEnum` for limited-value options. This naturally separates CLI parsing concerns from business logic implementation.

# Clap's Derive Pattern for Subcommand Handling

This example demonstrates how the `clap` Rust library structures CLI applications using derive macros. The key architectural pattern involves:

## Enum-Based Subcommand Organization

The example defines a `Commands` enum that represents different CLI operations:

```rust
enum Commands {
    Clone { remote: String },
    Diff { base, head, path, color },
    Push { remote: String },
    Add { path: Vec<PathBuf> },
    Stash(StashArgs),
    External(Vec<OsString>),
}
```

Each variant corresponds to a distinct command with its own arguments.

## Pattern Matching Dispatch

The `main()` function uses Rust's `match` statement to dispatch logic based on the parsed command:

"match args.command { Commands::Clone { remote } => { println!("Cloning {remote}"); }" demonstrates the routing approach.

## Nested Subcommands

For complex operations like `stash`, the pattern supports sub-subcommands through additional enums (`StashCommands`), allowing hierarchical command structures.

## Key Features Showcased

- **Declarative parsing** via `#[derive(Parser)]`
- **Argument validation** with attributes like `required = true`
- **Optional arguments** with sensible defaults
- **External subcommand** support for delegating to other programs

This design prioritizes type safety and compile-time validation while maintaining readable code organization.

# Error Handling Best Practices: thiserror & anyhow

## thiserror Enum Design

**Structure with variants for distinct failure modes:**
```rust
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum ConfigError {
    #[error("failed to read config file: {0}")]
    IoError(#[from] std::io::Error),
    
    #[error("missing required field: {field}")]
    MissingField { field: String },
}
```

Key principle: "Define custom error types with minimal boilerplate" to enable callers to understand what can fail.

## #[from] vs #[source]

**Use `#[from]`** when converting underlying errors into your enum variant automatically:
- Implements `From<T>` trait
- Enables seamless `?` operator usage
- Best for wrapping external crate errors

**Use `#[source]`** when preserving error chains without automatic conversion:
```rust
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DatabaseError {
    #[error("connection failed to {host}:{port}")]
    ConnectionFailed {
        host: String,
        port: u16,
        #[source]
        source: std::io::Error,
    },
}
```

This maintains the full error chain for debugging.

## thiserror for Libraries vs anyhow for Applications

| Aspect | thiserror (Libraries) | anyhow (Applications) |
|--------|----------------------|----------------------|
| **Purpose** | Structured, matchable errors | Quick error propagation |
| **User Control** | Callers handle specific variants | Errors logged/displayed to users |
| **Type Safety** | Preserves type information | Loses type detail intentionally |

As stated: "Use `thiserror` when writing a library...callers need to know what can fail. Use `anyhow` when writing application code where errors eventually get logged."

## Adding Context

**With anyhow's `context` method:**
```rust
load_config("app.json")
    .context("failed to load application config")?;
```

Provides human-readable chain output without creating new enum variants.

## Error Enum Granularity

**Avoid over-engineering:** "If you have 20 variants and callers always handle them the same way, you've over-engineered."

Group related failures together. Use `#[error(transparent)]` to wrap underlying errors when fine-grained variants don't add value.

## #[non_exhaustive] Pattern

Not explicitly covered in the source, but related principle: design enums to be extendable. The article emphasizes maintaining backward compatibility through thoughtful variant grouping.

## DO/DON'T Summary

**DO:**
- Always derive `Debug` for error types
- Preserve error chains with `#[source]` or `#[from]`
- Use `thiserror` in library public APIs
- Apply `anyhow` for internal application logic

**DON'T:**
- Expose `anyhow::Error` in library public APIs
- Create excessive error variants for identical handling
- Ignore error chains—"Losing context makes debugging painful"
- Mix concerns: keep libraries structured, applications flexible

## When to Split Crates

A 2025 study found that 61% of Rust developers hit the wall around 8,000 lines, right when one crate starts feeling like it's pretending to be three different projects. As your project develops, you might find that the library crate continues to get bigger and you want to split your package further into multiple library crates.

Key reasons to split include:
- Compilation times becoming a problem, and having multiple smaller crates means that most of the application does not need to be rebuilt when you make a change in one file. Or you might want to enforce more loose coupling between the application, and split the responsibility of various parts to separate teams.

## Best Practices for Library and Binary Crates

Divide your project into crates based on functionality (e.g., core logic, utilities, APIs). Define common dependencies in the root Cargo.toml for consistency.

For structure: If your workspace is for a library rather than an executable, simply set up the main crate for your project with cargo new <crate_name> --lib. Next, set up the crates that are dependencies for the main crate using cargo new with the --lib flag, which ensures those crates are compiled as dependencies for the main crate, not as programs by themselves.

## Key Considerations

Splitting crates has a cost: it means you need to define the interface well. Splitting crates out prematurely is probably not a good idea, but doing it too late risks that your code will depend on and use private interfaces that you don't want it to use.

Minimize tight coupling between crates to maintain modularity.

## Benefits of Workspaces

The crates in a workspace are meant to depend on each other. By sharing one target directory, the crates can avoid unnecessary rebuilding.

## Characterization Tests for Safe Refactoring

A characterization test is a test that characterizes the actual behavior of a piece of code, allowing you to take a snapshot of what it does and ensure that it doesn't change. The goal of characterization tests is to help developers verify that modifications made to a reference version of a software system did not modify its behavior in unwanted or undesirable ways.

## Why They're Important for Rust

Characterization tests are useful when you're refactoring some not-very-easily-tested code and don't want to break anything. Having comprehensive tests before refactoring is crucial, as tests act as a safety net to catch any behavioral changes you might accidentally introduce.

## Automated Verification in Rust

Recent research has focused on improving refactoring safety in Rust. A Rust Analyzer based design can provide fast, feature-rich extract-function refactoring for real Rust programs, while an optional verification pipeline can deliver machine-checked behavior preservation for safety-critical refactorings, making safe, semantics-preserving extract-method refactoring practical for everyday Rust development.

## Practical Approach

A practical solution is to start by adding characterization tests that capture existing behavior, then gradually refactor and improve test coverage. This allows you to safely make incremental changes while maintaining confidence that existing behavior is preserved.

# Clippy Lint Groups

Clippy organizes lints into distinct categories, each serving different purposes:

## Lint Groups Overview

| Group | Purpose | Recommendation |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| **Correctness** | Deny-by-default lints for outright wrong or useless code | Fix all issues; don't allow them |
| **Suspicious** | Code that is "sus" and should be fixed, though may be intentional | Fix or locally allow with justification |
| **Complexity** | Suggestions to simplify code while preserving semantics | Apply or allow case-by-case |
| **Perf** | Performance optimization suggestions | Usually easy to apply; recommended |
| **Style** | Idiomatic Rust writing conventions (most opinionated) | Apply for readability, but allow liberally if you disagree |
| **Pedantic** | In-depth checks for Clippy power users | Cherry-pick selectively; expect to use `#[allow]` frequently |
| **Restriction** | Lints that restrict certain Rust language features | Cherry-pick only; **don't enable the whole group** |
| **Cargo** | Suggestions to improve `Cargo.toml` | Useful for publishable crates |
| **Nursery** | Buggy or incomplete lints needing more work | Cherry-pick only; **don't enable the whole group** |
| **Deprecated** | Empty lints ensuring deprecated lint attributes still compile | Informational only |

## Key Guidance

- **Enable by default**: Correctness only (deny-by-default)
- **Cherry-pick cautiously**: Restriction, Nursery, Pedantic
- **Feel free to allow**: Style (subjective), Pedantic (overly strict)
- **Best practice**: Start with Correctness and Suspicious, gradually add others as needed

# CLI Error Handling & Exit Codes: Concrete Recommendations

## Exit Codes Strategy

The article establishes a **standardized exit code system** for scripting integration:

```rust
pub mod exit_code {
    pub const SUCCESS: i32 = 0;
    pub const GENERAL_ERROR: i32 = 1;
    pub const USAGE_ERROR: i32 = 2;
    pub const CONFIG_ERROR: i32 = 3;
    pub const IO_ERROR: i32 = 4;
    pub const PERMISSION_ERROR: i32 = 5;
    pub const NETWORK_ERROR: i32 = 6;
}
```

The pattern maps error types to specific exit codes, enabling downstream tools to programmatically respond to failures based on the root cause.

## Error Handling Architecture

**Two-tier error system** separates concerns:

1. **Domain errors** (library layer): Use `thiserror` for typed errors with context
   - `#[derive(Error, Debug)]` provides Display implementations automatically
   - Named variants like `ProjectExists`, `TemplateNotFound` communicate intent

2. **Application errors** (CLI layer): Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for convenient chaining
   - `with_context()` enriches errors with operational details
   - `bail!()` converts domain errors into Result types

Example from the guide:

```rust
std::fs::create_dir_all(&target_dir)
    .with_context(|| format!("Failed to create directory: {}", target_dir.display()))?;
```

## Mapping Errors to Exit Codes

The main function implements a **type-aware exit code mapper**:

```rust
fn determine_exit_code(error: &anyhow::Error) -> i32 {
    if error.downcast_ref::<std::io::Error>().is_some() {
        return exit_code::IO_ERROR;
    }
    if error.downcast_ref::<CliError>().is_some() {
        return exit_code::GENERAL_ERROR;
    }
    exit_code::GENERAL_ERROR
}
```

This approach inspects the error chain and selects appropriate codes without exposing underlying libraries to top-level logic.

## Separation of Parsing and Logic

The architecture enforces clean boundaries:

- **Clap derive macros** handle all argument parsing and validation
- **Business logic functions** receive only validated data
- **Error handling occurs in command functions**, not main

Commands like `cmd_build()`, `cmd_deploy()` return `Result<()>`, allowing main to centralize error reporting and exit code determination.

## Best Practice Quote

The guide emphasizes: *"Return meaningful exit codes for scripting"*—signaling that CLI tools must support automation workflows where calling processes evaluate exit status programmatically.
```

# Iterator Performance Advice Summary

Based on The Rust Performance Book's iterators chapter, here are the key recommendations:

**Allocation Avoidance**
The guide emphasizes returning `impl Iterator<Item=T>` rather than `Vec<T>` to prevent unnecessary allocations. "You should avoid calling `collect` if the collection is then only iterated over again." Instead, use `extend()` to add iterator elements to existing collections.

**Size Hints Matter**
Implementing `size_hint()` or `len()` on custom iterators allows `collect()` and `extend()` to pre-allocate memory more efficiently, reducing allocation overhead.

**Chaining Performance**
While convenient, `chain()` can underperform a single iterator in hot code paths. Similarly, combining `filter_map()` outpaces using `filter()` followed by `map()`.

**Chunking Optimization**
Use `chunks_exact()` instead of `chunks()` when slice length divides evenly by chunk size. Even with uneven divisions, `chunks_exact()` combined with remainder handling often performs better.

**Copied Data Types**
For small data like integers, `iter().copied()` may generate superior machine code compared to `iter()` alone, though verification through machine code inspection is recommended for confirmation.

These strategies collectively minimize unnecessary allocations and leverage compiler optimizations for better runtime performance.
```
</details></tool-use>

# When to Refactor vs. When NOT to Refactor

## **WHEN TO REFACTOR** (Green Signals)

**Strategic Timing:**
- "Before adding new features. When you're updating a module or extending functionality, it's smart to tidy up the existing code first."
- During framework or version migrations when touching large code sections
- After product releases when delivery deadlines are met
- Throughout code reviews when spotting problematic patterns

**Explicit Warning Signs:**
- Duplicated logic appearing in multiple places
- Single changes breaking multiple features (tight coupling)
- New developers struggling to understand variable names, file structures, or function purposes
- Code is difficult to understand or modify
- Adding new features takes longer than expected

## **WHEN NOT TO REFACTOR** (Red Signals—Avoid or Delay)

**Risky Situations:**
- **Without test coverage**: Refactoring without comprehensive automated tests dramatically increases bug risk
- **Under time pressure**: Pursuing "perfect" refactoring while facing delivery deadlines creates bottlenecks
- **Legacy code without tests**: Attempting large refactors on untested legacy systems is dangerous
- **Lack of understanding**: Refactoring code you don't fully comprehend risks introducing hidden defects

**Premature/Unnecessary Churn:**
- Refactoring code that works fine and isn't being modified frequently
- Pursuing perfection instead of meaningful incremental improvements
- Making large-scale overhauls simultaneously rather than small, testable steps
- Refactoring before understanding existing architecture and dependencies

**Key Principle**: Refactoring should be continuous and incremental, not a separate massive project.
```

## Key Resources

**proc-exit Crate**: The proc-exit crate demonstrates a common pattern where you call a `run()` function and then pass its result to `proc_exit::exit()`, which integrates with `std::io::Error`. This implements a main wrapper pattern that separates business logic from exit code handling.

**std::process::ExitCode**: ExitCode can be returned from the main function of a crate, as it implements Termination. It's recommended to return a type implementing Termination (such as ExitCode or Result) from the main function rather than calling std::process::exit().

**std::process::exit()**: This function never returns and terminates the process immediately, so no destructors on the current stack or any other thread's stack will be run.

## Exit Code Libraries

Several crates provide standardized exit codes:

- **exitcode**: The exitcode library provides BSD ecosystem exit codes, ready to be used in your application
- **sysexit**: It encodes the exit codes of sysexits(3) from OpenBSD (64–78), exit statuses used by bash(1), supplemented by codes created by shells when the command is terminated by a fatal signal
- **proc-exit**: Integrates with std::process and std::io::Error with a run function wrapper pattern

The search results contain practical examples and documentation for implementing exit codes properly in Rust CLI applications.

# Rust Module/Workspace Organization & Error Handling — Actionable Rubric (2025-2026)

## 1. Splitting a 40k-line single file into modules WITHOUT changing the public API

The mechanism that makes this a no-op for downstream code: the crate's public API is defined by *what is reachable via `pub` paths from the crate root*, not by which file an item lives in. Move items into files, then re-export them at their original paths.

**Procedure (incremental, compile-green at each step):**
1. Decide module boundaries by *domain cohesion* (types + their methods + closely-related free functions stay together), not by item kind. Avoid `types.rs` / `functions.rs` splits.
2. For each cluster, create `src/foo.rs` (modern file-as-module form) and physically move the code there.
3. In the root (`lib.rs`), add `mod foo;` and then **re-export to preserve old paths**: `pub use foo::{Bar, baz};` (or `pub use foo::*;` as a transitional step, tighten later).
4. Compile after each move. Run `cargo public-api` / `cargo semver-checks` to *prove* the API surface is byte-for-byte unchanged.
5. Keep `impl` blocks in the same module as the type they implement (Rust requires the type or trait to be local to the crate, not the module — but co-locating keeps navigation sane).

**DO**
- Use a **facade**: internal modules stay private (`mod foo;`), and a curated set of items is re-exported at the crate root with `pub use`. This is idiomatic and ubiquitous in Rust.
- Make moves mechanical and reversible; one commit per cohesive module.
- Verify with `cargo public-api`/`cargo semver-checks` that nothing leaked or disappeared.

**DON'T**
- Don't make the new submodules `pub mod foo;` if `foo` wasn't a public path before — that *adds* a new public path (a semver-relevant change). Keep `mod foo;` private and re-export only the intended items.
- Don't reorganize behavior and structure in the same commit.
- Don't split by syntactic category (all structs here, all fns there).

Sources: [Separating Modules into Different Files — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-05-separating-modules-into-different-files.html), [Re-exporting modules — Sling Academy](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/exporting-types-and-functions-in-rust-via-re-exporting-modules/), [Structuring large-scale Rust apps — Sling Academy](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/best-practices-for-structuring-large-scale-rust-applications-with-modules/)

## 2. `mod.rs` vs file-as-module

Since Rust 2018 (rustc 1.30), the compiler resolves a module `foo` to either `src/foo.rs` (+ optional `src/foo/` directory for its children) **or** the legacy `src/foo/mod.rs`.

**DO**
- Prefer the modern form: `src/foo.rs` for the module body, `src/foo/` for its submodules. This avoids a tree full of indistinguishable `mod.rs` tabs in your editor and is the community-preferred convention.

**DON'T**
- Don't mix the two styles within one crate without reason. Pick file-as-module and be consistent.
- Don't keep adding `mod.rs` files in new code just because old code uses them.

Sources: [Modules — The Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html), [module.rs vs mod.rs — Rust Internals](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/the-module-scheme-module-rs-file-module-folder-instead-of-just-module-mod-rs-introduced-by-the-2018-edition-maybe-a-little-bit-more-confusing/21977), [Rust module system — Shesh's blog](https://www.sheshbabu.com/posts/rust-module-system/)

## 3. Re-export / facade patterns to keep paths stable

**DO**
- Use `pub use internal::Type;` at the root so users import `crate::Type` regardless of internal layout — the layout becomes a free refactoring axis.
- Re-export third-party types you expose in your signatures (e.g. `pub use other_crate::Config;`) so consumers don't need to add that dependency themselves and version-skew is avoided.
- Consider a `prelude` module (`pub mod prelude { pub use ... }`) for the common-case imports of a large crate.

**DON'T**
- Don't expose deep internal paths (`crate::internal::detail::Thing`) as the public way to reach a type; that locks your internal structure into your semver contract.
- Don't glob-re-export (`pub use foo::*;`) in the final API — it leaks future additions unintentionally. Glob is fine as a *temporary* refactor scaffold only.

Sources: [Separating Modules into Different Files — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-05-separating-modules-into-different-files.html), [Re-exporting modules — Sling Academy](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/exporting-types-and-functions-in-rust-via-re-exporting-modules/)

## 4. Visibility discipline (`pub` vs `pub(crate)` vs private)

Everything is private by default. Visibility is your encapsulation tool; widen it deliberately.

**DO**
- Default to private. Promote to `pub(crate)` for items shared across modules but NOT part of the public API. Reserve bare `pub` for the genuine external contract.
- Use `pub(super)` / `pub(in path)` for narrowly-scoped sharing within a subtree.
- Mark fields private and expose accessors when you need future flexibility; make structs/enums `#[non_exhaustive]` if external matching/construction would otherwise freeze them.
- Audit the surface periodically with `cargo public-api`.

**DON'T**
- Don't reach for `pub` to silence "unused"/visibility errors during a refactor — use `pub(crate)`. Spurious `pub` is how internals accidentally become a semver contract.
- Don't expose struct fields you might want to compute or validate later.

Sources: [Managing Growing Projects — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-00-managing-growing-projects-with-packages-crates-and-modules.html), [Structuring large-scale Rust apps — Sling Academy](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/best-practices-for-structuring-large-scale-rust-applications-with-modules/)

## 5. Error handling — `thiserror` (libraries) vs `anyhow`/`eyre` (binaries)

The 2025/2026 consensus: **`thiserror` for libraries, `anyhow` (or `eyre`/`color-eyre`/`miette`) for binaries and application top-levels.** Libraries owe callers concrete, matchable error *types*; applications mostly log/display and want ergonomic propagation with context.

**DO (libraries)**
- Define a concrete `#[derive(thiserror::Error, Debug)]` enum as your public error type. It implements `std::error::Error` with zero boilerplate.
- Preserve the cause chain with `#[from]` (auto-`From` + enables `?`) or `#[source]` (keep the chain without auto-conversion, useful when you also carry context fields like `host`/`port`).
- Use `#[error(transparent)]` to forward a single wrapped error when a distinct variant adds no value.
- Add `#[non_exhaustive]` to the enum so adding variants later isn't a breaking change.

**DO (binaries / app top-level)**
- Use `anyhow::Result<T>` (or `eyre`) for `main` and internal app glue; attach `.context("...")`/`.with_context(...)` at each layer to build a human-readable trail.
- Use `color-eyre` or `miette` when the error is shown to an end user / CLI for nicer reports and diagnostics.

**DON'T**
- Don't put `anyhow::Error`/`eyre::Report` in a library's public signatures — it's type-erased, so callers can't match on cases.
- Don't drop the underlying cause (no bare `.map_err(|_| MyError::Whatever)` that discards `source`).
- Don't `derive(thiserror::Error)` in a binary that never exposes errors to callers — `anyhow` is less ceremony there.

Sources: [Designing Error Types with thiserror and anyhow — OneUptime (2026-01)](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-25-error-types-thiserror-anyhow-rust/view), [Rust Error Handling Guide 2025 — Markaicode](https://markaicode.com/rust-error-handling-2025-guide/), [anyhow vs thiserror vs snafu — DEV](https://dev.to/leapcell/rust-error-handling-compared-anyhow-vs-thiserror-vs-snafu-2003), [Error Handling — Luca Palmieri](https://www.lpalmieri.com/posts/error-handling-rust/)

## 6. Error enum design

**DO**
- One variant per *distinct failure mode the caller might handle differently* — message-only differences with identical handling should be merged.
- Write clear `#[error("...")]` messages with field interpolation (`{field}`, `{0}`); make them lowercase, no trailing punctuation, no "Error:" prefix (the chain adds context).
- Carry structured context in variants (`MissingField { field: String }`, `ConnectionFailed { host, port, #[source] source }`) rather than baking everything into a string.
- Add `#[non_exhaustive]` and prefer accessor methods over public fields for forward compatibility.

**DON'T**
- Don't over-engineer: "If you have 20 variants and callers always handle them the same way, you've over-engineered." Group related failures.
- Don't make the enum a giant catch-all `Other(String)` that destroys matchability.
- Don't nest deep error-enum hierarchies if a flat enum with `#[source]` chaining suffices.

Sources: [Designing Error Types — OneUptime (2026-01)](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-25-error-types-thiserror-anyhow-rust/view), [To panic! or Not to panic! — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-03-to-panic-or-not-to-panic.html)

## 7. Avoiding `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!`, and result propagation

Rule of thumb: **return `Result` when failure is an expected, recoverable possibility; panic only on programmer-bug invariants that should be impossible.**

**DO**
- Default to the `?` operator for propagation — clearer flow, better messages, gives callers options.
- Use `Result` combinators (`map`, `and_then`, `ok_or_else`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`) and `if let` / `let ... else` instead of unwrapping.
- If you must assert an invariant, prefer `expect("reason this is impossible")` over `unwrap()` — the message documents *why* it's safe; pair every such call with that justification (the "expect-as-documentation" convention).
- Reserve `unwrap`/`expect` for: tests, prototypes, and provably-infallible cases (e.g. parsing a hardcoded literal).
- Lint it: enable `#![warn(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used, clippy::panic)]` in library crates to catch regressions.

**DON'T**
- Don't `unwrap`/`expect` on fallible external I/O — HTTP, RPC, DB, file system, env. These fail in production.
- Don't `unwrap()` in library code at all in the success path; callers know better what to do with the error.
- Don't panic to signal ordinary recoverable conditions (missing config, bad user input) — that's a `Result`.

Sources: [To panic! or Not to panic! — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-03-to-panic-or-not-to-panic.html), [Using unwrap() is Okay — burntsushi](https://burntsushi.net/unwrap/), [Why only `expect` — The Coded Message](https://www.thecodedmessage.com/posts/2022-07-14-programming-unwrap/), [Don't Unwrap Options — corrode.dev](https://corrode.dev/blog/rust-option-handling-best-practices/)

## 8. Workspace / multi-crate split (the next step after module split)

Surveys cited in 2025 reporting note developers commonly hit organizational/compile-time pain as a single crate grows (around the 8k-line mark a crate often "feels like three projects").

**DO**
- Split into a Cargo **workspace** when you need: faster incremental builds (a change in one crate doesn't rebuild the rest, shared `target/`), enforced loose coupling, or team ownership boundaries.
- Split by *functional layer*: `core` (domain logic, `thiserror` error types), `utils`, adapters/`api`, and a thin top-level `bin` crate that uses `anyhow`/`eyre`.
- Centralize shared dependency versions in `[workspace.dependencies]` in the root `Cargo.toml`; reference with `dep.workspace = true`.
- Keep the binary crate thin; put logic in library crates so it's testable and reusable.

**DON'T**
- Don't split crates *prematurely* — you pay an interface-definition cost and lose easy cross-module refactoring. But don't wait so long that code starts depending on internals you didn't want public.
- Don't create cyclic crate dependencies (Cargo forbids them anyway) — design clean layering.

Sources: [Cargo Workspaces — The Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch14-03-cargo-workspaces.html), [Organize Rust projects for faster compilation with workspaces — InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4050654/organize-rust-projects-for-faster-compilation-with-cargo-workspaces.html), [Workspace — Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/organization/workspace.html)

---

### One-line summary of the playbook
Split the 40k-line file by domain into modern `foo.rs` modules kept *private* (`mod foo;`), re-export the intended items at the crate root (`pub use`) to keep every public path byte-identical, verify with `cargo public-api`/`cargo semver-checks`; keep internals `pub(crate)`; expose a `thiserror` enum (granular-but-not-excessive, `#[source]`/`#[from]` chains, `#[non_exhaustive]`) as the library's error type while `main`/app glue uses `anyhow`/`eyre` with `.context`; replace `unwrap` with `?`/combinators and lint `clippy::unwrap_used`; graduate to a Cargo workspace once compile times or coupling justify the interface cost.

# Rust Idiom, Style & Maintainability Rubric (2025–2026)

## 1. Clippy lint groups

**DO**
- Keep `correctness` and `suspicious` at deny/warn — these catch real bugs, not style. Correctness is deny-by-default already; don't `allow` it.
- Take `perf` and `complexity` wholesale — fixes are usually mechanical, semantics-preserving, and free wins.
- **Cherry-pick** from `pedantic`. High-value picks: `missing_errors_doc`, `missing_panics_doc`, `must_use_candidate`, `cast_precision_loss`/`cast_possible_truncation`, `struct_excessive_bools`, `needless_pass_by_value`, `semicolon_if_nothing_returned`. Configure in `[lints]` of `Cargo.toml` (workspace-level via `[workspace.lints]` + `lints.workspace = true`), not scattered `#![allow]`.
- Selectively allow noisy pedantic lints rather than disabling the group: e.g. `module_name_repetitions`, `must_use_candidate` if they generate churn.
- For libraries, lean harder into `pedantic`; for app/binary crates, be more permissive.

**DON'T**
- Don't enable the whole `nursery` or `restriction` group — nursery lints are buggy/incomplete and restriction lints are mutually contradictory by design (cherry-pick only, e.g. `restriction::unwrap_used` in libs).
- Don't blanket-enable `pedantic` and then drown the file in `#[allow]` attributes — that's a code smell that you adopted the group without curating it.
- Don't treat `style` as gospel — it's the most opinionated group; allow liberally where your team disagrees.

Source: [Clippy lint groups](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/clippy/lints.html), [Clippy index](https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html), [Useful Clippy lints](https://rtaw.co.uk/posts/clippy-lints/)

## 2. Clones & allocations

**DO**
- Borrow first (`&T`, `.iter()`) and clone only at the point you genuinely need ownership.
- Prefer `.copied()` over `.cloned()` for `Copy` types — better codegen.
- Return `impl Iterator<Item=T>` from functions instead of `Vec<T>` to avoid allocating at boundaries.
- Use `extend()` into an existing collection rather than `collect()` + merge.
- Implement `size_hint()`/`len()` on custom iterators so `collect`/`extend` pre-allocate.
- Accept `impl AsRef<str>` / `&str` / `&[T]` in signatures rather than `String`/`Vec<T>` when you only read.

**DON'T**
- Don't `.clone()` to silence the borrow checker reflexively — it hides ownership-model problems and costs allocations in loops.
- Don't `.collect()` into a `Vec` only to immediately iterate it again.
- Don't clone inside `for x in vec.clone()` / map iteration — iterate by reference.

Source: [Effective Rust Item 9](https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/iterators.html), [Perf Book: Iterators](https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/iterators.html), [Avoiding accidental clones](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/avoiding-accidental-clones-in-loops-over-vectors-or-hash-maps/)

## 3. Iterators vs index loops

**DO**
- Prefer iterator chains (`map`/`filter`/`fold`/`sum`/`for_each`) — zero-cost, elide bounds checks, enable LLVM vectorization.
- Fuse `filter().map()` into `filter_map()`; use `chunks_exact()` over `chunks()` when length divides evenly.
- Use `for_each` for side effects, `fold`/`sum` for aggregation.

**DON'T**
- Don't reach for `for i in 0..v.len() { v[i] }` index loops — they reintroduce bounds checks and block optimization. (Exception: when you genuinely need the index or multiple-array striding, where `chain()` can also underperform in hot paths — measure.)

Source: [Perf Book: Iterators](https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/iterators.html), [Effective Rust Item 9](https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/iterators.html)

## 4. Newtype pattern

**DO**
- Wrap primitives in single-field tuple structs (`struct UserId(u64)`) when mixing same-underlying-type values would be a bug — ids, currencies, validated-vs-raw input.
- Use newtypes to kill argument bloat: distinct types make wrong-order args a compile error.
- Encapsulate validation in the constructor so an instance is proof of validity (parse, don't validate).
- Implement `Deref` **only** when the newtype adds capability while keeping the full inner surface; **skip** `Deref` when the point is to restrict/safen the API.

**DON'T**
- Don't auto-derive/forward every trait — be intentional; reflexive boilerplate defeats the safety purpose.
- Don't newtype trivially when a plain type alias or no wrapper is clearer (aliases give zero safety).

Source: [Effective Rust Item 6](https://www.lurklurk.org/effective-rust/newtype.html), [Rust Design Patterns: Newtype](https://rust-unofficial.github.io/patterns/patterns/behavioural/newtype.html), [Comprehensive Rust](https://google.github.io/comprehensive-rust/idiomatic/leveraging-the-type-system/newtype-pattern.html)

## 5. Builders & argument bloat

**DO**
- Use a builder when a constructor has many optional/defaulted params; `build(self)` validates and returns the final type.
- Combine with **typestate** (marker types) to make required fields a compile-time requirement.
- When params grow past ~4-5 or several share a type, group them into a config/options struct or newtypes.

**DON'T**
- Don't build a builder for a 2-field struct with no optionality — that's ceremony.
- Don't pass long positional argument lists of same-typed primitives (swap-prone).

Source: [Newtype/typestate patterns (Microsoft)](https://microsoft.github.io/RustTraining/rust-patterns-book/ch03-the-newtype-and-type-state-patterns.html), [Mastering Rust Newtypes (SoftwareMill)](https://softwaremill.com/mastering-rust-patterns-vol-1-rust-newtypes/)

## 6. Derive usage

**DO** — derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq/Eq`, `Hash`, `Default` where they make sense; derive `serde::{Serialize,Deserialize}` rather than hand-writing.
**DON'T** — don't derive `Clone`/`Copy` on large types just for convenience (hides cost), and remember derive-macro crates (`serde_derive`, `thiserror`) look "unused" to static scanners — exempt them from machete.

## 7. Dependency hygiene in workspaces

**DO**
- Centralize versions in `[workspace.dependencies]` and reference with `dep.workspace = true` for consistency.
- Run `cargo machete` (stable, no nightly) to find unused deps; wire it into pre-commit/CI. `cargo machete --fix` prunes.
- Run `cargo deny` for license/advisory/duplicate-version policy and `cargo audit` for known CVEs.
- Add a `machete` ignore list for proc-macro/derive false positives.

**DON'T**
- Don't let each crate pin its own divergent versions of shared deps.
- Don't carry dependencies "just in case" — every dep is transitive-CVE surface and binary bloat.

Source: [cargo-machete](https://github.com/bnjbvr/cargo-machete), [Cargo 1.90 dev cycle](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/10/01/this-development-cycle-in-cargo-1.90/)

## 8. Refactoring safely (behavior-identical)

**DO**
- Pin behavior **before** touching code: write characterization / golden-master tests that snapshot current output (e.g. `insta` snapshots, golden-master harnesses).
- Capture the public surface: `cargo public-api` / `cargo semver-checks` to prove the API didn't drift.
- Refactor in small, individually-compiling, individually-testable steps; commit each.
- Use the compiler + `rust-analyzer` rename/extract-function refactorings (mechanically safe), then re-run the full suite.
- Add mutation testing (`cargo-mutants`) to confirm the tests actually constrain the behavior you're preserving.

**DON'T**
- Don't refactor untested legacy code without first adding the characterization net.
- Don't bundle behavior changes into a "refactor" commit — keep them separate so review can verify zero functional delta.

Source: [Characterization testing](https://cloudamite.com/characterization-testing/), [Golden master regression in Rust](https://blog.anp.lol/rust/2017/08/18/golden-master-regression-in-rust/), [REM equivalence toolchain](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.19207v1)

## 9. When NOT to refactor (avoid needless churn)

**Red flags that a refactor is churn, not value — DON'T proceed:**
- Code works, is stable, and **isn't being touched** for upcoming features — no behavioral or maintenance pressure.
- **No test coverage / you don't fully understand the code** — refactoring blind injects defects.
- **Under deadline pressure** chasing "perfect" structure — creates bottlenecks for no shipped value.
- Large simultaneous overhaul instead of small incremental steps — high blast radius, unreviewable.
- Purely cosmetic reshuffling (renaming, reordering, re-styling) that Clippy/rustfmt didn't ask for and that generates large diffs reviewers must re-verify.
- Refactoring driven by "I'd write it differently" rather than a concrete signal (duplication, tight coupling causing cross-feature breakage, confusing names slowing onboarding, features taking longer to add).

**Green-light signals to actually refactor:** duplicated logic in multiple places; one change breaks several features (coupling); newcomers can't parse names/structure; adding features is slow. Refactor *just before* extending the relevant module, incrementally, with tests in place.

Source: [Tembo: When to refactor and avoid mistakes](https://www.tembo.io/blog/code-refactoring), [freeCodeCamp: Refactor complex codebases](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/how-to-refactor-complex-codebases/)

---

### One-line TL;DR
Curate (don't bulk-enable) Clippy `pedantic`; borrow before you clone and prefer iterators returning `impl Iterator`; use newtypes/typestate to kill argument bloat; centralize workspace deps and prune with `cargo machete`/`deny`/`audit`; and only refactor tested, understood code that has a concrete pressure signal — pin behavior with characterization tests and public-API snapshots first, and skip cosmetic churn that just inflates diffs.

# Rubric: Maintainable Rust CLI Applications (2025-2026)

Source-backed DO/DON'T rules. Validated against ripgrep, cargo, uv, and jj source layouts plus the clap derive reference and Rain's Rust CLI recommendations.

## 1. Crate split: thin binary, fat library

**DO** put a near-empty `main.rs`/`src/bin/<name>.rs` and move all logic into `lib.rs` + modules. `main` should only: parse args, call a `run()` entry, map the result to an exit code. Rationale: `main` can't be unit-tested; everything in a library can. This is the canonical "separation of concerns" refactor from the Rust Book ch12.
**DON'T** grow a god `main.rs`. As responsibilities accumulate it "becomes more difficult to reason about, harder to test, and harder to change without breaking one of its parts."
- https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch12-03-improving-error-handling-and-modularity.html

**DO** split into a workspace once the library is large and reusable. ripgrep is a workspace of 9 member crates where the `rg` binary just coordinates library crates (`grep-regex`, `grep-searcher`, `ignore`, etc.); jj and uv split `jj-lib`/library crates from `jj-cli`/`uv` binary. Rationale: forces a clean API boundary between engine and CLI, and speeds incremental compile.
- https://deepwiki.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep
- https://deepwiki.com/jj-vcs/jj/1-overview

## 2. clap derive: App-is-a-struct, commands are an enum

**DO** make the top-level a `#[derive(Parser)]` **struct** holding `#[command(subcommand)] command: Commands` plus a flattened `GlobalOpts`. Make `Commands` a `#[derive(Subcommand)]` enum.
**DON'T** make the top-level App itself an enum. "While it is possible to make `App` an enum with all the subcommands, in my experience this design has always come back to bite me" — it blocks you from later adding global options cleanly.
- https://rust-cli-recommendations.sunshowers.io/handling-arguments.html

**DO** use `#[clap(flatten)]` liberally to break long option lists into small reusable structs living in their own files (e.g. an `OutputOpts` in `output.rs`). Benefits: reusable option groups, file-level organization, and bundling complex arg sets so they pass through your code as one value.
**DO** mark cross-cutting flags (`--color`, `--verbose`, `--config`) with `#[clap(global = true)]` so they work after any subcommand.
**DO** use `#[derive(ValueEnum)]` for fixed-choice options so clap validates them at parse time.
- https://rust-cli-recommendations.sunshowers.io/handling-arguments.html
- https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/index.html

## 3. Command module organization (the hybrid layout used by the big four)

**DO** adopt the hybrid `commands/` directory pattern that cargo, uv, and jj all converge on:
- **One file per standalone subcommand** — cargo's `src/bin/cargo/commands/` has `build.rs`, `add.rs`, `check.rs`, etc., one per command.
- **A subdirectory per command *family*** with nested subcommands — jj groups `bookmark/`, `git/`, `operation/`, `workspace/` while keeping simple commands (`commit.rs`, `log.rs`, `diff.rs`) as flat files; uv groups `pip/`, `project/`, `python/`, `tool/`, `auth/` and keeps `venv.rs`, `publish.rs` flat.
- https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/tree/master/src/bin/cargo/commands
- https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj/tree/main/cli/src/commands
- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/tree/main/crates/uv/src/commands

**DO** give every command module a uniform two-function shape, like cargo: a `cli()` that builds/returns the command's args, and an `exec()` that runs it. Rationale: a uniform contract makes a single dispatch `match` trivial and makes adding a command a copy-paste-rename operation.
**DON'T** cram every subcommand's args and logic into one enum + one giant `match` in `main`. Use a thin dispatcher that delegates to each module's `exec`/`run`.

**DO** decide subcommand-vs-flags deliberately. cargo is **subcommand-based** (each verb = a child command: `cargo build`, `cargo clean`); ripgrep is **single-command** (one `rg`, behavior driven by flags). Pick subcommands when verbs do genuinely different jobs; pick flags when there's one job with modes.
- https://kbknapp.dev/cli-structure-01/

## 4. Separate parsing from business logic

**DO** treat clap structs as a parse boundary only. Parse → convert into your own validated domain types → call business functions that know nothing about clap. "Business logic functions receive only validated data." Rationale: business logic stays testable without constructing clap matches, and you can add a second frontend (library API, MCP, etc.) later.
**DON'T** thread `ArgMatches` or `Cli` structs deep into your engine.
- https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-07-rust-cli-clap-error-handling/view

## 5. Argument validation

**DO** let the type system and clap do the first layer: declare args as `u16`, `PathBuf`, `IpAddr`, `ValueEnum`, etc., so clap rejects bad input and exits with usage error before your code runs.
**DO** use clap's `value_parser` for richer constraints (ranges, custom parse fns) so invalid input fails at parse time with a good message — not deep in logic with a panic.
**DON'T** re-validate what clap already guarantees, and don't push semantic checks (e.g. "file must exist") into clap parsers when they belong in command logic returning a typed error.
- https://blog.logrocket.com/command-line-argument-parsing-rust-using-clap/
- https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/_derive/index.html

## 6. Exit codes

**DO** return `ExitCode` (or `Result`) from `main` — both implement `Termination` — rather than calling `std::process::exit()`. `std::process::exit()` skips destructors on all stacks, so reserve it for the outermost wrapper if at all.
- https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/process/struct.ExitCode.html
- https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/fn.exit.html

**DO** follow convention: `0` success, `1` general failure, `2` usage/CLI-parse error (clap already exits `2` for parse errors). For richer scripting, adopt the BSD `sysexits(3)` codes via the `exitcode`, `sysexit`, or `proc-exit` crates instead of inventing numbers.
- https://rust-cli.github.io/book/in-depth/exit-code.html
- https://github.com/rust-cli/proc-exit
- https://docs.rs/exitcode/latest/exitcode/

**DO** centralize mapping from error type to exit code in one place (a `determine_exit_code(&Error)` that downcasts the error chain), keeping the rest of the code ignorant of exit numbers.
**DON'T** scatter `std::process::exit(n)` calls throughout command logic — return errors and let the top-level wrapper assign the code.
- https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-07-rust-cli-clap-error-handling/view

## 7. Error handling (two-tier)

**DO** use a two-layer error model: `thiserror` typed enums in the library/domain layer (named variants like `TemplateNotFound` carry intent and are matchable for exit-code mapping), and `anyhow::Result` with `.with_context(...)` at the CLI/application layer for ergonomic chaining and human-readable context.
**DON'T** use `anyhow` inside reusable library crates (callers lose the ability to match on errors); don't `unwrap()`/`panic!` on user-input errors — surface them through the `Result` → exit-code path so the message is clean and the code is meaningful.
- https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-07-rust-cli-clap-error-handling/view

## 8. Help, UX, and build-time artifacts

**DO** write generous `///` doc comments on every arg/subcommand — they become `--help`, which is your primary documentation.
**DO** generate man pages and shell completions at build time via a `build.rs` (ripgrep's approach) so docs never drift from the arg definitions.
- https://www.shuttle.dev/blog/2023/12/08/clap-rust
- https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep
